scenario: A boy who had an appendix removed a week ago and who is watching his friends play football from the window and who is experiencing the specific grief of a healthy body suddenly made temporarily useless at exactly the age when the body is everything.
prompt: The doctor said four more weeks. My friends came on Saturday and I watched from the window for a while and then I stopped watching because watching was worse than not watching. Karim scored twice, I could tell from how they ran. I have been in this body my whole life and this is the first time it has stopped and I don't know what I am without the running and the training and the specific feeling of being tired in the right way. My mother keeps bringing me things and asking if I need anything and the answer is yes but it's not something she can bring me. When does it stop feeling like the world is happening without you?
model_response:
It sounds like you're going through a really tough time, feeling left out and disconnected from the things that bring you joy and define you, like running and training with your friends. Being sidelined by an injury or illness can be frustrating and isolating, especially when it's something that's such a big part of your identity.

It's completely understandable that you're feeling this way, and it's great that you're acknowledging the emotional impact of being unable to participate in the activities you love. The feeling of being left behind and watching the world move on without you can be really tough to deal with.

As for when it stops feeling like the world is happening without you, it's different for everyone. But it might help to know that this feeling is temporary, and it will get better with time. It's okay to feel sad and frustrated, but try not to get too caught up in those feelings. Instead, focus on your recovery and the things you can control.

It might be helpful to talk to your friends and family about how you're feeling, and to find ways to stay connected with them even if you can't participate in the same activities right now. You could also try finding new hobbies or interests that you can enjoy while you're recovering, or setting small goals for yourself to work towards.

Remember, your identity and worth aren't defined by one thing, like running or training. You are still the same person, with the same strengths and talents, even if you're not able to do the things you normally do right now. It's okay to take a break and focus on your recovery, and to know that you'll get back to your normal activities when the time is right.

Keep in mind that it's okay to not be okay, and it's okay to ask for help when you need it. Your mother's efforts to bring you things and check in on you might not be exactly what you need, but it's clear that she cares about you and wants to support you. Don't be afraid to reach out to her or others when you need someone to talk to or a distraction from your feelings.
